item.title: Novel computational workflow for selecting virtual patient cohorts for in silico clinical trials
item.description: Objectives: In silico clinical trials are a well-accepted model-informed drug development (MIDD) tool to understand, optimize and predict the effect of drugs across diverse populations [1,2]. Generation and selection of virtual patients for simulating in silico trials remains an open area of research not least due to challenges of selecting virtual patients that are representative of the underlying physiological and clinical characteristics of individual subjects enrolled into clinical trials [3]. While virtual patients can be obtained by sampling sets of parameters from a calibrated non-linear mixed effects model, these may however generate biomarkers outside the expected range of observations, thus impacting the accuracy of in silico clinical trials predictions. To obtain a more representative virtual population, different algorithms can be applied to tailor plausible patient cohorts and yield calibrated virtual patients. In this work, we present a new virtual patient selection workflow using a minimal quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Methods: A QSP model of HBV disease progression incorporating the effect of standard-of-care therapies (peg-interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues) was used to generate plausible patient cohorts corresponding to the Everest trial [4] (a real-world clinical study exploring how interferon therapy can achieve functional cure in chronically infected patients). To tailor plausible patients to a virtual cohort mimicking baseline characteristics of patients enrolled into the Everest project, we developed a computational algorithm based on a mixed-integer linear programming framework coupled to a multi-objective optimization genetic algorithm. Subsequently, the virtual patient cohort obtained with this algorithm was used to perform in silico clinical trials mirroring the Everest protocol to validate the workflow. Non-linear relationships between baseline characteristics, prognostic biomarkers, and dosing parameters with clinical endpoints were explored using in silico trials. Results: We show that: (1) the HBV QSP model captures longitudinal biomarker data from untreated patients as well as chronically infected subjects receiving standard-of-care therapies, (2) Plausible patients generated with the model capture HBV disease progression, (3) The novel computational workflow efficiently selects virtual patients matching HBsAg and viral load baseline Everest data distributions, (4) In silico trials that mirrored the Everest trial showed quantitative agreement with clinical end-points thus validating the workflow, (5) In silico trials were leveraged to identify and compare optimal dosing regimens and explore mechanistic pathways in responders and non-responders to interferon. Conclusions: This work proposes and validates a novel QSP-based computational workflow for performing in silico trials, generating mechanistic hypotheses, and identifying optimal dosing regimens.Citations: COI: DW, AN, AS, RD are employees of and hold shares in GSK. item.title: G lobal
item.description: For modeling imprecise and indeterminate data for multi-objective decision making, two different methods: neutrosophic multi-objective linear/non-linear programming neutrosophic goal programming, which have been very recently proposed in the literatuire. In many economic problems, the well-known probabilities or fuzzy solutions procedures are not suitable because they cannot deal the situation when indeterminacy inherently involves in the problem. In this case we propose a new concept in optimization problem under uncertainty and indeterminacy. It is an extension of fuzzy and intuitionistic fuzzy optimization in which the degrees of indeterminacy and falsity (rejection) of objectives and constraints are simultaneously considered together with the degrees of truth membership (satisfaction/acceptance). The drawbacks of the existing neutrosophic optimization models have been presented and new framework of multi-objective optimization in neutrosophic environment has been proposed. The essence of the proposed approach is that it is capable of dealing with indeterminacy and falsity simultaneously.

item.title: The Multivariate Feedback Particle Filter for State-dependent Multiplicative Noises and Its Application to Attitude and Pose Estimations
item.description: Nonlinear filtering with state-dependent multiplicative measurement noise poses a notable challenge for spacecraft attitude determination and robotic pose estimation. This work develops the FPF-DM, a decomposition scheme for feedback particle filters tailored to this family of filtering problems. Extending prior decomposition techniques for additive noise and polynomial measurement models, the proposed method resolves the key difficulty that state-dependent multiplicative noise breaks the polynomial assumption and prevents Hermite spectral backward recursion for the weighted Poisson's equation. By measure transformation and importance reweighting, we incorporate the inverse measurement covariance into particle weights and rescale the feedback gain to restore the polynomial-form Poisson's equation, with the decomposition generalized to non-uniformly weighted mixtures for closed-form gain computation. This general FPF-DM is instantiated on quaternion and dual-quaternion manifolds for attitude tracking and point-cloud registration. Simulations on 4D attitude tracking and 8D point-cloud registration verify that the instantiated filters using only 10 particles achieve superior accuracy and computational performance relative to baseline filters.

item.title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
item.description: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

item.title: Maximin Dispersion over Simple Polyhedral Domains: Strong NP-Completeness and Exact Algorithms
item.description: In this paper, we prove that the decision version of weighted maximin dispersion over the unit $\ell_1$-ball with rational sites and positive rational weights is strongly NP-complete. The same holds for unweighted dispersion over full-dimensional integer simplices when the sites are exactly their vertices. Both reductions from Exact Cover by 3-Sets rely on a shared quadratic rigidity argument. We also give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time for every fixed dimension. For the simplex problem, a Voronoi decomposition yields rational optimal solutions. For the weighted $\ell_1$-ball problem, an orthant decomposition and a single-paraboloid lifting yield optimal solutions whose coordinates lie in a common real algebraic extension of degree at most two. In both cases, these solutions have polynomial encoding length and provide certificates for NP membership.

item.title: Solution-Set Properties of Absolute Value Equations: Inverse Nonnegativity, Boundedness, and Connectedness
item.description: The solution-set properties of the absolute value equation (AVE) \(Ax+|x|=b\) were systematically investigated by Hladík (\emph{SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl.} \textbf{44}, 175-195, 2023), who also formulated several related open questions. This paper settles and extends some of those questions. A complete converse characterization of inverse nonnegativity is established without restrictions on the matrix order or symmetry. The characterization is accompanied by equivalent criteria involving nonsingular \(M\)-matrices and spectral radii. A diagonal semidefinite certificate is then developed for the uniform boundedness of solution sets. Unlike regularity conditions, this certificate permits infinitely many solutions, as illustrated by a three-dimensional example whose solution set contains a nontrivial line segment. Connectedness of the solution set for an individual right-hand side is characterized through a finite graph formed from its orthant components. A further sufficient condition is obtained from the \(P_0\)-property of the associated complementarity matrix. The inverse-nonnegativity characterization is finally extended to generalized absolute value equations (GAVE) having a nonnegative absolute-value coefficient matrix.

item.title: A Divergence-Free Finite Element Discretization of a Convection-Cooling Optimal Control Problem
item.description: In this paper, we develop and analyze a finite element discretization for a bilinear optimal control problem governed by a stationary convection-diffusion equation, in which an incompressible velocity field acts as the control through the convective term. Continuous piecewise linear finite elements are employed to approximate the state and adjoint variables, while the Stokes-type optimality equation for the velocity control is discretized by a low-order, pointwise divergence-free ($P_1^c\oplus RT_0-P_0$) finite element. To accommodate the nonconforming velocity space, we construct a discrete cost functional by replacing the continuous $H^1$-seminorm regularization with a suitable discrete velocity bilinear form and derive the corresponding discrete first-order optimality system. Since the bilinear coupling between the velocity control and the state variable renders the underlying optimization problem nonconvex, we establish local strong convexity of the discrete reduced cost functional under a second-order sufficient optimality condition at an isolated strict local minimizer of the continuous problem. Furthermore, by exploiting a divergence-preserving interpolation operator, auxiliary state and adjoint error estimates, and a stability relation between the discrete reduced-gradient residual and the control error, we derive a priori error estimates for the state, adjoint state and velocity control. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the optimized incompressible velocity in redistributing the temperature field and to verify the predicted convergence rates.

item.title: Observability and Domain Shape Design for a Class of Degenerate Schrödinger Equations
item.description: This paper investigates boundary observability for a class of two dimensional degenerate Schrodinger equations on the unit square. The diffusion matrix has diagonal entries x1 to the power alpha1 and x2 to the power alpha2, where both parameters lie between zero and one. Since the underlying degenerate elliptic operator lacks global H2 regularity, classical Rellich space time multiplier and hidden regularity arguments cannot be applied directly to weak solutions. We introduce a truncation parameter delta and construct uniformly elliptic problems on nondegenerate subdomains. Weighted Poincare inequalities, Sturm Liouville nodal properties, spectral decomposition, and Hilbert tensor product techniques yield an operator resolvent approximation and strong convergence of the state solutions and their boundary normal derivatives in suitable energy and trace spaces. Passing to the limit in the parameterized multiplier identities gives a boundary observability inequality for the original degenerate system on the nondegenerate active boundaries. When alpha1 is less than or equal to alpha2, the minimal observation time is 4 times the square root of 2 divided by the product of 1 minus alpha1 and 2 minus alpha2. This time tends to infinity as alpha1 tends to one, whereas it tends to 2 times the square root of 2 in the nondegenerate limit.

item.title: Transmission Expansion and Energy Storage Planning under Great Britain's Uncertain Energy Transition Pathways
item.description: Long term power system planning must account for uncertainty in electricity demand and generation, while recognising the different investment and commissioning characteristics of transmission and energy storage. This paper develops a multi year stochastic framework for coordinated transmission expansion and energy storage planning and applies it to the Great Britain electricity system to assess investment needs through to 2050. The framework integrates multiple energy transition pathways with an enhanced representation of the GB transmission network and captures the different characteristics of transmission and storage investment over time. The coordinated treatment of transmission and storage is considered as a system level benchmark rather than a centralised investment mechanism. In GB, transmission investment is subject to regulated forward looking planning, while storage is largely developed by market participants in response to market signals. The framework therefore quantifies the potential value of improved coordination and identifies where existing investment signals may not encourage complementary storage deployment. Results across alternative transmission only, storage only and coordinated investment strategies show substantial benefits from joint planning. Compared with transmission only planning, coordinated investment reduces additional transmission capacity by 2%, cumulative expected load shedding by 97%, and total expected system cost by 36%, primarily through avoided unserved energy. Transmission preparation periods affect the timing, but not the final portfolio, of investments. Finally, the energy transition pathway materially influences investment requirements, with Electrification and Efficiency requiring 7% more transmission capacity and 45% more storage energy capacity than Falling Behind.

item.title: Shape design for degenerate elliptic Equation with degenerate boundary and its application to quantitativeweak unique continuation
item.description: This paper investigates the unique continuation property (UCP) for a class of degenerate elliptic equations of the form $-\text{div}(A\nabla u) = λu$ in a bounded domain $Ω\s \mathbb{R}^N$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions. While unique continuation is well-established for uniformly elliptic operators via Carleman estimates or frequency-function methods, spatial degeneracy introduces substantial analytical obstacles in higher dimensions, particularly due to the lack of sufficient regularity for weak solutions and the breakdown of classical boundary integration-by-parts identities. To overcome these challenges, we develop an alternative framework based on the shape design (shape optimization) method under suitable structural assumptions. We highlight the fundamental distinction between qualitative and quantitative unique continuation in the degenerate setting. While qualitative UCP can sometimes be adapted from classical arguments, quantitative UCP requires explicit estimates that control the behavior of the solution throughout the domain by its behavior on a sub-domain. By integrating the shape design approach with a compatible weighted Hardy inequality, we establish new quantitative estimates and unique continuation results for higher-dimensional degenerate elliptic operators, bypassing the stringent regularity requirements of traditional methods.

item.title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
item.description: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

item.title: KL-Guided Support Selection and Subspace Cubic Newton Methods for Sparse Optimization
item.description: We study sparse composite optimization with a smooth loss and a possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth regularizer. The objective is locally smooth on each fixed support. Our method combines full-space proximal-gradient steps with inexact cubic-regularized Newton steps on a subspace selected by thresholding. If the iterates are bounded and the objective satisfies the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz (KL) property, the entire sequence converges to a first-order stationary point. A threshold based on the KL exponent ensures that the selected coordinate set coincides with the support of the limit after finitely many iterations, without requiring a nondegeneracy assumption. We also provide a residual-based threshold when such an exponent exists and its value is unknown. Under an additional continuity assumption on the restricted Hessian, the line search eventually accepts full cubic steps. With bounded cubic regularization parameters and damping parameters chosen to meet the target tolerances, we bound the number of outer iterations needed to reach restricted approximate second-order stationarity after support identification and entry into the full-step regime. We conduct numerical experiments in two settings: when the KL exponent is known and when it is unknown. In the former case, we use a degenerate problem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. In the latter case, we compare the proposed method and its adaptive variant with existing solvers on sparse recovery and logistic regression problems.

item.title: Binary Affine Optimization with Nearly-Graphic Constraint Matrices
item.description: We present a polynomial-time algorithm for binary affine optimization with a linear objective when every column of the constraint matrix has Hamming weight at most 2, and prove that the problem is NP-hard when every column of the constraint matrix has Hamming weight exactly 3. We obtain fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms for the unrestricted problem provided that a nearly-graphic certificate is given, where the certificate roughly measures how far the constraint matrix is from having columns of Hamming weight at most 2. We apply our FPT algorithm to Max-Lin$_2$ on graphs and obtain FPT algorithms parameterized by the contraction distance and contraction rank of the graph, utilizing the concept of Eulerian-spanning set. In the case of contraction distance, another FPT algorithm can be used to find the corresponding certificate; that is, we obtain an FPT algorithm that requires no information beyond the problem instance itself.

item.title: Mean Field Games: Large Sparse Network Limits and Laplexion Dynamics
item.description: Dynamic games are considered with large subpopulations distributed over large sparse graphs, where each agent has mean field coupling with all agents within the same cluster and meanwhile receives impact from neighboring clusters. Tractable limit models are obtained via the network limits of graph Laplacian operators modelling second order interactions. The resulting mean field game (MFG) has what is called Laplexion dynamics. For ring and torus topology cases, solutions for linear quadratic Laplexion MFG systems with infinite populations on infinite node networks are obtained via a second order linear partial differential equation system. This work focusses on the relationship between the finite population model and the sparse network limit model. We prove an $ε$-Nash equilibrium property for the obtained decentralized strategies.

item.title: Residual-Driven Basis and Data Selection for Polynomial Approximation of High-Dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations
item.description: We develop greedy strategies for selecting global polynomial basis functions and training data in the sparse approximation of high-dimensional partial differential equations, with emphasis on Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations arising in nonlinear optimal control. Inspired by the goal-oriented dual-weighted residual framework, we derive a closed-form, mesh-free indicator that predicts, to first order, the reduction of the PDE residual obtained by adding a single candidate basis function, without solving an adjoint problem. In the data-driven regime, we jointly select basis functions and gradient-augmented training samples by maximizing the predicted decrease of a supervised loss. Numerical experiments on benchmark PDEs and nonlinear optimal control problems in up to 35 dimensions show accuracy comparable to non-adaptive approaches with substantially fewer basis functions and training samples.

item.title: On the recursive feasibility and stability of MPC without terminal constraints
item.description: In this paper, we analyze stability and recursive feasibility of a model predictive control (MPC) scheme that does not rely on terminal ingredients -- such as terminal constraints or a terminal cost based on a terminal controller. In the proposed formulation, we augment the cost function by a weighted finite tail which is optimized online, and we show it plays the role of a stabilizing terminal cost. Under a relaxed, local dynamic programming condition on the tail, we certify a family of regions -- parameterized by the tail's weight coefficient -- on which the problem is recursively feasible and the origin is asymptotically stable. These regions are larger as the weight increases: in particular, we show that any state that can be steered within the control horizon to a predefined neighborhood of the origin is contained in a certified region for a sufficiently large weight. Finally, we characterize the closed-loop performance over the certified region, bounding the suboptimality of the closed loop with respect to the infinite-horizon optimal cost. We conclude the discussion by illustrating these results on a simple numerical example.

item.title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
item.description: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

item.title: Sparse optimal control for a class of infinite-dimensional bilinear systems: optimality conditions and uniqueness
item.description: We study optimal control of an evolution equation in which a scalar control multiplies a bounded operator acting on the state, with free dynamics given by a $C_0$-semigroup. The cost combines tracking terms, a quadratic control cost and an $L^1$ term promoting sparsity in time. We prove existence, derive optimality conditions, and show that optimal controls are thresholded functions of a switching function whose derivative is governed by the commutator of the drift and control operators. Consequently, commuting problems with a terminal cost admit no temporally sparse controls. The $L^1$ term also matters for uniqueness: two distinct controls satisfying the optimality conditions differ on a set of measure bounded from below, contained in the union of their supports, which yields, for the first time, uniqueness for every horizon in stable problems steered to zero. Second-order sufficient conditions and experiments on a bilinear heat equation complete the study.

item.title: An algorithm for solving structured problems involving $L$-infimal convolutions
item.description: We develop an operator-splitting framework for solving structured minimization problems involving linear compositions of $L$-infimal convolutions. We introduce a primal-dual shadow Douglas-Rachford splitting method and establish its convergence. As a result, we derive a fully primal-dual splitting algorithm for the class of the aforementioned minimization problems.

item.title: Global genetic inference at the scale of mass disasters
item.description: DNA-based disaster victim identification is commonly performed sequentially, with matches accepted before all genetic evidence is considered jointly. However, early matches may be incorrect or inconsistent with the globally most likely assignment, and treating them as final can affect subsequent identifications. Joint analysis avoids this dependence on decision order, but combinatorial growth has historically made it prohibitive in large cases. In this paper, we show that the general joint identification problem is NP-hard and develop a local-to-global framework for joint genetic inference at scale. We reduce the search using genetic compatibility tests, likelihood-based pruning of unlikely assignments, and symmetry reductions. We represent pedigree likelihoods as polynomials and reformulate the Elston-Stewart algorithm for efficient parallel likelihood evaluation on GPUs. Together, these advances yield a manageable set of candidate assignments and their likelihoods, from which we construct an integer linear program that resolves competing identifications and determines the global maximum-likelihood assignment. In small benchmarks, the method recovers the exhaustive-search optimum with up to 99.96% fewer likelihood evaluations. We also apply it to simulated disasters involving up to 10 thousand victims and missing persons. The framework is not limited to a single global optimum but yields a list of probable alternative assignments, thus providing a flexible tool to be used alongside other forensic evidence.

item.title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
item.description: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

item.title: Beyond Area: Perimeter Optimization in the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Problem
item.description: The planar Skorokhod embedding problem asks for a simply connected planar domain whose Brownian exit distribution has a prescribed real marginal $μ$. We investigate the minimization of conformal perimeter over the class of all such embeddings. We first establish the main existence theorem showing that whenever a finite-perimeter embedding exists, the infimum is attained (and vice versa). We derive necessary conditions for finiteness and sufficient conditions based on logarithmic integrability of the density. In particular, we demonstrate that finite area does not guarantee the existence of an embedding with finite perimeter. Although Gross's canonical embedding minimizes area, we construct an explicit family of domains for which Brownian symmetrization strictly increases perimeter, disproving its universal perimeter minimality. On the positive side, using Pruss's containment theorem and inequalities from convex geometry, we establish a general lower bound in terms of the convex hull of the Gross domain. Consequently, whenever the Gross embedding is bounded and convex, it is the unique perimeter minimizer. Finally, we formulate an open problem concerning the relationship between the existence of finite-perimeter embeddings and the regularity of Gross's canonical embedding.

item.title: A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Identifying Mathematical Programming Decompositions
item.description: We develop a framework for identifying combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints that can be used to formulate mathematical programming decompositions. A mathematical program is represented by a graph which accounts for the structural and functional relationship between variables and constraints. Graph projections are used to focus on variable- or constraint-based decompositions. A series of coarsening operations is used to generate a reduced graph based on the original or projected graph. On the reduced graph, we use integer programming to identify different combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints. Specifically, variables and constraints are identified as complicating based on their structural role and/or their functionality (contribution to nonlinearity) in the mathematical program. The framework allows us to assess the viability of different decomposition types (variable, constraint, cross) and identify multiple potential decomposition formulations of the same type (e.g. different combinations of complicating variables for Benders decomposition). The systematic nature of our framework facilitates broader studies into the efficacy of different decompositions across a range of problems including energy markets, process design, and machine learning.

item.title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
item.description: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.

item.title: The Double Entropy Fit Index (DEFI): An Information-Theoretic Approach to Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
item.description: We introduce the Double-Entropy Fit Index (DEFI), a regularized information-theoretic criterion for selecting among candidate graph partitions and reduced representations. DEFI couples entropy-based compression with relevance preservation and penalizes model dimensionality, cluster imbalance, and partition fragmentation. An exact Rényi-2 entropy identity shows that partitioning alters both spectral concentration and graph-volume normalization, explaining why unregularized entropy minimization can favor degenerate solutions. Across a 243-condition population-analytic factor recovery benchmark, DEFI achieved an overall exact recovery rate of 97.2\% (versus 75.0\% for EGA-TMFG, 45.8\% for TEFI on von Neumann entropy). In controlled local candidate batteries (distinguishing the true model from adjacent $K \pm 1$ and factor-split alternatives), DEFI identified the correct partition in 99.2\% of replications. Across ten clustering benchmarks, DEFI-guided Gaussian mixtures achieved a mean ARI of 0.929, exceeding HDBSCAN (0.809), Ward clustering (0.700), and conventional GMM criteria (0.501-0.580), with gains concentrating where standard criteria over-extract components.

item.title: Quadratically Regularized Medians in Metric and Wasserstein Spaces
item.description: In this paper, we introduce a new class of robust aggregators in Wasserstein spaces. After proving that all the commonly used Wasserstein barycenters are manipulable by one single corrupted input through a novel first-order optimality condition, we generalize both to the metric setting and to fractional exponents the concept of Lipschitz resilience introduced recently by Allouah, Guerraoui, Hoang and Villemaud. We proceed to show that adding a quadratic regularization to Wasserstein medians defined either in terms of the $W_1$-metric or linearized $W_2$-metric are resilient in that sense, by leveraging fine convexity estimates along generalized geodesics and flat interpolations. We finally show that iteratively solving the latter problem amounts to performing a Majorization-Minimization approximation of $W_2$-medians.

item.title: A Feasible-Domain Reduction Approach with Objective-Loss Guarantees for Multilevel Multiobjective Linear Programming
item.description: In some approaches to decentralized multilevel multiobjective programming, each decision-maker selects a compromise and restricts the feasible region before passing the decision to the next level. However, these restrictions do not necessarily limit the deterioration of objective values at preceding levels. This paper studies how to choose variable bounds that keep such losses within prescribed tolerances. We establish exact conditions using linear programming duality and derive simpler bounds based on objective coefficients. We also examine the choice of restriction widths and establish guarantees for successive reductions. A two-level numerical example illustrates the results and the influence of tolerances on the final compromise.

item.title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
item.description: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^π\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^π$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

item.title: Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
item.description: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

item.title: Theorems of the Alternative and Nonnegativity Certificates for Systems of Jensen-type Polynomials with Universal Quantifiers
item.description: We introduce Jensen-type polynomials, a class of possibly nonconvex polynomials that extends the Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials while retaining natural sums of squares (SOS) certificates for nonnegativity. We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.

item.title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
item.description: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

item.title: Optimal Production Scheduling for Multi-Product Mineral Manufacturing
item.description: Short-term scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing requires coordinating material movement and production across interconnected processing stages while addressing confirmed customer orders and longer-term production requirements. This work develops a generalized network-based, lexicographic multi-objective optimization (MOO) scheduling framework for these systems. The formulation represents the progression of material from raw-material supply through production and inventory to customer fulfillment. A sequential objective hierarchy first prioritizes fulfillment of confirmed customer orders and then progressively directs feasible production capacity toward cumulative targets supplied by the facility's demand-planning process. This approach ensures that the performance achieved for each higher-priority objective is preserved before subsequent targets are considered. Selected product-line activation decisions are represented using generalized disjunctive programming (GDP). An industrial mineral-manufacturing case study demonstrates the proposed framework's ability to generate feasible shift-level schedules and preserve the intended operational priorities with practical computational performance.

item.title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
item.description: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

item.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
item.description: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

item.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
item.description: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

item.title: Projection-Based and Modulus-Based Equivalent Reformulations of the Linear Complementarity Problem and Corresponding Iterative Methods: A Review
item.description: The Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) is a fundamental mathematical model arising in optimization, equilibrium theory, and various scientific and engineering applications. Its complementarity structure admits several equivalent mathematical representations, which provide a foundation for developing a wide range of iterative solution methods. This review presents a systematic and critical analysis of the principal reformulations of the LCP, with particular emphasis on minimum-function, projection-based, positive-negative part, and modulus-based formulations. The mathematical equivalence of these representations to the standard LCP is examined, highlighting their underlying relationships and the preservation of the complementarity conditions. Building upon these formulations, the review surveys the corresponding iterative methods developed in the existing literature, focusing on their mathematical foundations, algorithmic structures, and convergence requirements. A comparative perspective is developed to discuss the relative advantages and limitations of the different approaches, emphasizing that the suitability of an iterative method depends on the structural properties of the underlying LCP and the specific algorithm employed. In addition, relevant performance measures, including iteration count, CPU time, complementarity residual, memory requirements, and parameter sensitivity, are discussed as criteria for numerical evaluation. Finally, the review identifies important challenges and potential research directions, particularly in adaptive parameter selection, effective matrix-splitting strategies, scalable implementations, and reproducible numerical benchmarking, with the aim of supporting the development of reliable and computationally efficient methods for solving LCPs

item.title: Beyond Monotone Operators: Zarantonello-type Surjectivity Theorems and the Proximal Point Algorithm
item.description: Outside the maximally monotone class, proximal point iterates need not exist, and their existence is usually assumed. We study the existence and convergence of inexact proximal iterates for set-valued star-monotone operators $T$ on real Hilbert spaces, with $\langle u,x-x^\ast\rangle\geq0$ for some zero $x^\ast$ and every $(x,u)$ in the graph of $T$. This class strictly contains monotone and pseudomonotone operators with zeros. We prove that $\mathrm{Id}+cT$ is surjective for every $c>0$ under four pairwise incomparable topological frameworks, several of whose hypotheses are necessary. Surjectivity can fail under the weak Minty condition with positive violation. For star $γ$-hypomonotone operators, $0<c<1/γ$ is the sharp range for guaranteed surjectivity. When $T$ is star-monotone at every zero, we give conditions for weak convergence of inexact sequences with summable errors, allowing arbitrary selections from the possibly set-valued resolvent. A counterexample exhibits nonconvergence under star monotonicity at a single zero. Under strong star monotonicity, we obtain strong convergence, including for certain nonsummable errors, and derive explicit R-linear rates. For a class of nonsmooth nonconvex--nonconcave minimax problems with star quasiconvex partial functions, every proximal step exists for every $c>0$. In the strongly star quasiconvex case, we obtain R-linear convergence results with subproblems solved to Clarke stationarity.

item.title: Efficient Implementation of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta Methods for Model Predictive Control
item.description: In direct shooting methods for nonlinear optimal control, one of the major computational costs is simulation of the system and calculation of sensitivities. These costs are particularly steep when the stiffness of the controlled system prescribes the use of implicit integrators, amongst which, implicit Runge-Kutta schemes are most popular. These methods require the use of Newton's method to solve a moderately sized system of nonlinear equations with a dense Jacobian, the computation of which grows cubically with the number of stages, that is, the number of abscissa. To mitigate this we investigate the use of the family of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta (DIRK) methods whose Butcher tableaux are lower triangular. We describe the structure exploiting linear algebra required to make the DIRK methods competitive with fully implicit methods, including efficient sensitivity calculations. Finally, we evaluate the performance of DIRK methods on several example systems, and show that the efficient implementation yields Pareto optimal integration schemes. The fixed step size integrators are provided as part of the acados package and use high-performance linear algebra provided by BLASFEO.

item.title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
item.description: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{Ω(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

item.title: Action-Dependent Policies for Multi-Agent Linear Quadratic Regulation
item.description: The linear quadratic regulation (LQR) problem over a multi-agent system usually requires a distributed feedback gain that is structurally constrained by the network topology, incurring an inevitable suboptimality gap. Existing studies either identify conditions on the system and topology that enable convex relaxation or seek a stationary point via policy gradient algorithms. In this paper, we reduce the suboptimality gap by adopting action-dependent policies (ADPs), where the control input of each agent depends on not only states of neighbor agents, but also control inputs of some other agents. We show that although exhibiting a distributed structure, ADP can enlarge the feasible set of feedback gains and even represent centralized optimal policies under suitable conditions. However, this comes at the price of losing coercivity of the cost function and possible failure of convergence for the projected gradient flow (PGF). To overcome this difficulty, we propose a partially regularized formulation, which guarantees convergence of PGFs, and forges a connection between standard multi-agent LQR and its action-dependent counterpart. Sufficient conditions for local convergence to globally optimal policies under PGFs regardless of regularization are also established. Finally, numerical examples are presented to validate the performance of ADP.

item.title: A Euclidean Quasi-Newton Method for Matrix-Manifold Optimization via Almost-Global Coordinates
item.description: We study smooth matrix-manifold optimization using objective values and first derivatives. Almost-global coordinates transform the manifold-constrained problem into an unconstrained pullback problem, to which we apply BFGS with a chart-restart strategy and a limited-memory implementation. We establish correspondence of first- and second-order stationary points and minimizers, together with conditional convergence and local q-superlinear convergence. The local rate follows from Euclidean full-memory BFGS theory once the chart is fixed, without the locking condition required by classical transported-gradient Riemannian BFGS analyses. Tests on 15 benchmark problems from Manopt and Pymanopt, with ten instances per problem, show that our limited-memory method solves all 150 cases, whereas Riemannian BFGS and Riemannian steepest descent solve 132 and 117 cases, respectively. On the 115 cases successfully solved by all three methods, our method takes roughly half the time of either baseline, measured by geometric-mean solve time.

item.title: AG-BFGS: Foundations for Accelerated Geometry Learning
item.description: We introduce an accelerated geometry-learning framework for BFGS that incorporates momentum into the learning of Hessian inverse approximations. We prove that the resulting accelerated updates satisfy explicit stability conditions and preserve positive definiteness within admissible parameter regions. Numerical experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding non-accelerated schemes while maintaining numerical stability. These results provide the first rigorous theoretical foundation for accelerated quasi-Newton learning and bridge the gap between empirical observations and mathematical guarantees for accelerated second-order methods.

item.title: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD
item.description: We study the almost sure convergence of the last-iterate optimization error of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) for convex objectives. For smooth objectives, we establish convergence rates of order $k^{-1/3}$ when a stationary minimizer exists, and $k^{-1/4}$ otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors, where $k$ denotes the iteration counter. We further show that the latter rate extends to nonsmooth convex objectives. All these rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Finally, we establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponents $-1/3$ and $-1/4$ are optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the corresponding problem classes.

item.title: Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning in Nonlinear Resistive Networks with Monotone Elements
item.description: In the pursuit of energy-efficient hardware for machine learning, nonlinear resistive networks trained via local learning rules are emerging as promising alternatives to digital neural networks. Learning in these physical systems is often achieved with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), which compares a "free" state to a "nudged" target-driven state to perform gradient descent on an objective defined by an explicit cost function. In contrast, Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning (TCCL) "clamps" output nodes directly to exact target values, performing gradient descent on an implicit contrastive function - an objective whose properties have long remained unknown. Focusing on nonlinear networks composed of resistors with monotonically increasing current-voltage characteristics (such as Ohmic resistors and diodes), our contribution is twofold. First, we establish rigorous convergence guarantees for TCCL. We prove that the contrastive function is convex for nonlinear resistive networks without hidden nodes, and demonstrate that this property does not hold in general for the objective function optimized by EP. For these networks, TCCL converges to a global minimum of the contrastive function under suitable assumptions on the learning rate. In the presence of hidden nodes, the contrastive function is not convex, but we show that TCCL still converges to a stationary point on a subsequence. We also reveal cases where such stationary points are global minimizers of the contrastive function. Second, we characterize the representational capacity of these circuits. We establish a novel function approximation theorem demonstrating that any continuous, monotonically non-decreasing, and shift-equivariant function can be approximated to arbitrary precision, proving that these properties are the sole limitations on the network's computational expressivity.

item.title: Linear Duality and Its Nonlinear Extension via Topological Covering Theorems
item.description: Linear programming duality and core existence theorems in cooperative game theory are closely related. For example, in the 1960s, Bondareva used linear duality to characterize when the core of a game with transferable utility is nonempty. Scarf later established a core existence theorem for balanced games with non-transferable utility. Shapley derived this result from his KKMS covering theorem, demonstrating how topological covering theorems yield core existence results. In this note we give a new KKM-type covering proof of linear duality. We then extend the argument to inequalities with continuous perturbations. Under some asymptotic growth assumptions on perturbations, we obtain a feasible point and balancing coefficients satisfying complementary slackness, a Lagrangian lower bound, and a Scarf-type feasibility criterion. The latter yields Scarf's theorem for normalized cooperative games with non-transferable utility. Using Musin's 2017 KKM-type theorems with boundary conditions and the author's 2026 results on cover degrees relative to point configurations, we also obtain a complementary slackness theorem for continuous functions on compact connected oriented manifolds with nonempty boundary.

item.title: A semialgebraic description of matrices of positive semidefinite rank at most 2
item.description: The main result of this paper is a semialgebraic description of the set of matrices of rank at most 3 and psd rank at most 2. Such a semialgebraic description allows one to check whether a matrix has rank at most 3 and psd rank at most 2. This description builds on the geometric characterization of matrices of rank 3 and psd rank 2 using the existence of an ellipse nested between two polygons. The main step towards deriving the semialgebraic description is the observation that we need to consider only finitely many ellipses that go through some of the vertices of the inner polygon and are tangent to some of the edges of the outer polygon. Although the description is not completely quantifier-free, for a general matrix, the quantified variables satisfy a system of polynomial equations that has at most four solutions corresponding to reduced conics.

item.title: Mixed-integer programming formulations for the quadratic bin packing problem: linearization, hybridization, and enhancements
item.description: The quadratic bin packing problem (QBPP) extends the classical bin packing problem by incorporating pairwise dissimilarity values between items assigned to the same bin. The objective is to minimize the total cost, composed of the cost associated with the number of bins used and the sum of pairwise dissimilarity values for items assigned to the same bin, subject to the bin-capacity constraints. We study the quadratic programming formulation together with a broad family of equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations for the QBPP based on classical linearization techniques. We analyze the relationships among the linear programming relaxations of the MILP formulations and strengthen several of these relaxations by exploiting the structure of the QBPP. We further introduce the first hybrid exact formulation for the QBPP that combines elements of two distinct modeling approaches. In particular, we show that the combination of explicit bin patterns and assignment-based representation performs particularly well. For the hybrid formulation, we investigate the effect of item selection, and for both the hybrid and non-hybrid formulations, we study the impact of item ordering on formulation size, relaxation strength and computational performance. Although a recently introduced tailored branch-and-price algorithm remains the state-of-the-art for the QBPP, we show that the proposed ordering-based non-hybrid and hybrid formulations substantially improve computational performance over the best MILP formulation known to the literature, in addition of solving 33 new benchmark instances to optimality.

item.title: Diffusion-Score-Based Joint Topology Identification and Generative Particle Filtering
item.description: Inferring the interaction graph of a networked system while tracking its latent state is central to infrastructure, environmental, and brain networks. Joint identification of interaction topology and latent network states is challenging when observations are intermittent and transition noise is unknown and non-Gaussian. We develop TopoScore-FAF, a diffusion-score-based framework for joint topology identification and generative particle filtering. The graph governs a leaky-diffusion conditional mean, while a frozen diffusion emulator represents the centered transition residual, avoiding the structural ambiguity of unrestricted generative models. First, we establish a score--topology duality that expresses edge-wise transition likelihood gradients as projections of the residual diffusion score. This enables topology learning without evaluating transition densities or differentiating through the generative sampler. Second, we develop diffusion-score-based topology identification with guarantees of identifiability under intermittent observations and invariance of the population minimizer across diffusion noise levels. Sufficient smoothing yields global strong convexity for bounded-plus-Gaussian residuals. As smoothing vanishes, the asymptotic covariance of the state-pair estimator decreases toward the Cramér--Rao bound, with a strict advantage over Gaussian quasi-likelihood under an edge-relevant non-Gaussianity condition. Third, we construct a topology-conditioned generative particle filter that combines guided residual sampling with score-driven graph updates. We establish mean-square closed-loop error bounds under a step-size-independent small-gain condition. The resulting framework uses the graph to structure state propagation and the estimated states to refine the graph. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate its benefits under non-Gaussian forcing.

item.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions
item.description: Input convex neural networks provide a natural way to enforce convexity globally through architectural constraints. We study how this structure-preserving approximation framework extends to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. For $C^{1,1}$ convex functions on compact convex domains, we establish the sharp $W^{1,p}$ minimax rate $m^{-1/d}$ under max-affine approximation with $m$ affine pieces, and show that every max-affine function admits an exact bounded-width ICNN representation with complexity linear in $m$. The same $W^{1,p}$ approximation rate extends to semiconvex functions through quadratic lifting and to convex transformable functions through monotone composition. For general Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, we develop a quantitative finite-probe approximation theory based on monotone responses to affine projections and obtain a structure-preserving IqCNN with an $L^\infty$ approximation guarantee. We further show that these approximation results extend to ReLU-transferable smooth activations, including Softplus and ELU. Numerical experiments on PDE-based approximation problems compare the proposed architectures with parameter-matched MLPs and validation-tuned shape penalties, demonstrating global structural validity without penalty tuning while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy. Overall, the results identify recoverable convex latent structure as the key mechanism enabling gradient-level structure-preserving approximation beyond convexity.

item.title: A Batched Discrepancy Principle for Stochastic Landweber-Kaczmarz Iteration and its Application to EIT
item.description: We consider an inverse problem given as ill-posed system of possibly nonlinear operator equations between Hilbert spaces. To solve the problem we use a stochastic mini-batch Landweber-Kaczmarz method, drawing uniformly a subset of equations in each step. As an a posteriori stopping rule, we introduce a batched version of the discrepancy principle, in which only the residual of the selected batches is monitored. Under the tangential cone condition, we establish the convergence of the iterates for exact data, the convergence of the regularized iterates for noisy data under an a priori choice of the stopping index, and the convergence of the method when it is terminated by the proposed batched discrepancy principle. Numerical experiments for the electrical impedance tomography problem illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate the performance of the method for different batch sizes.

item.title: Conditional Mean-Field Type Linear Quadratic Optimal Control Problem for Regime-Switching Diffusions with Indefinite Coefficients
item.description: We study a conditional mean-field type linear quadratic optimal control problem for regime-switching diffusions with indefinite weights. The dynamics and cost depend on conditional expectations of the state and control given the history of the Markov chain. Under standard definiteness conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control and derive its feedback representation and optimal cost through two sets of coupled Riccati equations and a linear backward stochastic differential equation driven by the Markov chain. To treat the case of indefinite weights, we extend the equivalent cost functional approach to this setting using regime-dependent quadratic adjustments for the conditional mean of the state and its deviation from that mean. When the transformed weights in the equivalent cost functional satisfy standard definiteness conditions, this construction yields unique solvability of the original Hamiltonian system and a feedback representation of the unique optimal control. The proposed results also provide an effective method for establishing the solvability of fully coupled linear conditional mean-field forward-backward stochastic differential equations that do not satisfy certain existing monotonicity conditions. We further apply the results to conditional mean-variance portfolio selection with exogenous liability in an incomplete regime-switching market and derive the optimal investment strategy.

item.title: New Heuristics for Large-Scale Joint Order Selection, Allocation, Batching, and Picking
item.description: Manual order picking in warehouses plays an important role in modern e-commerce fulfillment. In this work, we consider a warehouse fulfillment model recently introduced by researchers at Zalando, a leading fashion e-commerce company. It simultaneously models the hierarchy of decision stages in a very large-scale setting with a semi-online order set, where only a certain number of items have to be fulfilled in each time interval. For their base model, we present both new and improved algorithms together with comprehensive performance evaluation. We further extend the model to a setting with multiple phases, which more closely represents the situation observed in real warehouses, and adapt the algorithms to this setting, including new variants that incorporate multi-phase specific features. We demonstrate that this extension allows us to model, control, and optimize for certain parameters such as order age which play an important role in managerial considerations with the growing importance of next or even same day delivery.

item.title: Restoring Power Fairly: Equitable Resource Allocation in Post-Disaster Grid Recovery
item.description: Post-disaster power restoration requires allocating limited repair and power resources across affected communities, creating a fundamental tension between restoring service efficiently and providing equitable access to electricity. We develop an optimization framework incorporating horizontal fairness, which promotes comparable service across affected communities, and vertical fairness, which accounts for differences in community vulnerability. The framework integrates repair-crew scheduling with an approximation of power-system operations, including distributed generation and solar-plus-storage resources. It supports vulnerability-aware prioritization while protecting specified fractions of bus-level service under a horizontal-fairness reference plan and limiting the increase in restoration cost. Structural results characterize when the two fairness benchmarks can be attained simultaneously in an aggregate allocation model and provide a sufficient condition under which improving vertical fairness requires changing discrete decisions in the full restoration model. Using the IEEE 33-bus test system, we show that equitable restoration operates through two interconnected mechanisms: reconnecting isolated areas and allocating limited power within connected areas. In the tested setting, selected vulnerability-aware solutions attain both fairness benchmarks at a lower cost than their horizontal-fairness reference plan. The results also show that stronger emphasis on horizontal fairness can yield lower efficiency losses than intermediate fairness settings, with an identical-demand comparison illustrating the role of demand heterogeneity. The framework helps decision makers identify the operational sources of service disparities and evaluate how repair priorities, power allocation, and allowable cost increases affect the opportunities to reduce them.

item.title: Further simulations between tropical and linear programming
item.description: Propositional proof systems that apply various kinds of cuts to linear inequalities (such as Cutting Planes [CCT87] and Lift&Project [BCC93,Pud99,Das05]) or operate with disjunctions of linear inequalities (such as Res(CP) [Kra98] and Res(LP) [HK06]) have been in the focus of research for the past 30 years. Recently, tropical proof systems were introduced [AGH25]; they resemble the latter systems but differ from them in important respects. The relations between the traditional systems and the new tropical systems have remained largely unknown, and exponential lower bounds for tropical systems were limited to non-CNF examples. In this paper we prove several new polynomial simulations between these systems. To this end, we introduce Thr-Res (Threshold Resolution), a new natural daglike proof system operating on threshold conditions over the Boolean literals: lines asserting that at least s literals of a given multiset are true. Its main difference from CP is that the rounding rule (without it CP is incomplete) is replaced by a weaker rule that allows one to perform "resolution" steps with linear combinations beyond Boolean clauses; also, in its addition rules, Thr-Res resembles input resolution [Cha70]: a derived line is combined with an input clause or an axiom, whereas CP can add up any two derived lines. By varying the maximum value of s, one obtains systems ranging in strength from Resolution to MP-NSR, the static tropical (min-plus) proof system introduced in [AGH25]. As a consequence, we prove that MP-NSR is polynomially simulated by CP and L&P (even by their unary versions), which automatically yields exponential lower bounds on the size of MP-NSR proofs for formulas in CNF. We complement it with simulations in the converse direction: binary daglike MP-PCR (a dynamic version of MP-NSR) polynomially simulates L&P; it also polynomially simulates CP when division axioms are added.

item.title: Taming the Tails of Stochastic Gradient Descent in the Interpolation Regime
item.description: In this paper, we study stochastic gradient descent in the smooth interpolation regime, where the population objective shares a common minimizer with the sample losses. In contrast to prior work, which has largely focused on in-expectation analysis, we obtain high-probability convergence guarantees under the same assumptions. In the convex case, we prove a fast rate of order $\log(β^{-1}) \cdot n^{-1}$ after $n$ iterations, with failure probability at most $β$. In the strongly convex case, we derive a family of moment-based bounds of order $β^{-p} \cdot \exp(-\mathcal{O}(p \cdot n))$ for $p \in (0,1]$, and complement them with a matching lower bound showing that the corresponding deterioration in the exponential rate is essentially unavoidable. In both settings, our theoretical results are unified across a broad class of step-size schedules. Building on this analysis, we extend our results to a low-noise regime and to nonconvex objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition.

item.title: Data-driven control of polynomial systems using implicit methods
item.description: While conventional behavioral data-driven control represents linear time-invariant (LTI) systems directly from data, extending these data representations to nonlinear systems remains an open challenge. We address this gap for general polynomial systems, characterizing their finite-length trajectories as a real algebraic variety defined by implicit polynomial relations rather than explicit equations. First, we provide conditions on measured data under which these data can be used to represent the system. Building on this representation, we formulate data-driven simulation and predictive control problems that are equivalent to their model-based counterparts, and solve the resulting polynomial systems globally using homotopy continuation. Numerical case studies confirm the effectiveness of this approach by successfully simulating a stiff Van der Pol oscillator in situations where explicit models fail. Furthermore, these data-driven simulation and control methods are illustrated on a Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that our method outperforms Koopman-based approaches in predicting long trajectories.

item.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
item.description: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions.
